items.article_search_text: ‘Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?’ 7NEWS brings you the latest local news from Australia and around the world. Stay up to date with all of the breaking sport, politics, entertainment, finance, weather and business headlines. Today's news, live updates & all the latest breaking stories from 7NEWS. Australian Formula One star Oscar Piastri will start from 10th on the gird for the Sao Paulo grand prix after Lando Norris put his McLaren on pole position for the third year in a row. It was a wild Saturday (Sunday AEDT) at Interlagos in tough ‌conditions after a long delay caused by torrential rain, and extra mechanical considerations for many drivers. George Russell qualified second fastest for Mercedes, 0.204 slower, but dropped down the ‌grid due to a five-place penalty, with his newly-crowned world champion teammate Kimi Antonelli replacing him alongside last year’s race winner and champion. Ferrari’s ‌Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop due to power unit changes, which meant Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson will start third and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg fourth. “The big shock there is Oscar Piastri,” Sky Sports commentator David Croft said. “He won’t be continuing in this qualifying session”. With the rain getting heavier and leaving no chance for anyone to improve on their times in the final phase, the clock ticked down for the last five minutes without a car on track. “Today is about getting on ‌pole. It doesn’t ‌really matter how you ⁠do it, so very pleased with that,” Norris said after a qualifying that started ​and was then halted for nearly an hour and a half. Russell was furious not to be fastest, wanting to make a statement despite knowing he had a penalty but having to abort his quick lap when he came up behind Williams’ Alex Albon. “Mate, you told me to back off! What the hell?,” he shouted over team radio after realising his day was done. “P2. I don’t ⁠want to be P2. I want to be P1.” Red Bull’s four-time champion ​Max Verstappen, with a 30 place grid penalty due to power unit changes, sat out the second phase that was red-flagged when Haas debutant Rafael Camara crashed. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who will also be starting at the back of the grid ​due ​to engine penalties amounting to an impossible 65 place ​drop, also went out. There was then a further delay to clear ‌debris before the decisive third phase. Conditions had eased in Q2, with double world champion Fernando Alonso leaning on his experience and the first to switch to intermediates. Camara earlier had the home crowd roaring when he reached the second phase but fellow-Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto had a nightmare for the second year running when he went off and qualified last. Bortoleto slid into the tyre wall with seven minutes to go ​but returned to the track and made his way back to the pits where the damage proved too extensive to ​fix in the time available. Both Alpines ⁠also went out at the first hurdle along with the two Cadillacs and Aston Martin’s ​Lance Stroll. Journalist from Australian news agency, Australian Associated Press.

items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri has lost his points finish in the Mexican Grand Prix after the stewards penalised him for a collision. 2nd November 2026, 0:10 2nd November 2026, 9:05 | Written by Keith Collantine Advert | Become a Supporter & go ad-free The McLaren driver tangled with Arvid Lindblad while trying to overtake the Racing Bulls driver. The stewards issued the McLaren driver a 10-second time penalty which drops him from seventh place to 15th. The stewards ruled Piastri was not entitled to be given racing room when he tried to pass Lindblad on the outside of the corner and could have avoided the collision. “On the approach to turn one the driver of car 81 [Piastri] attempted an overtake on the outside of car 41 [Lindblad],” the stewards explained. “Car 81 was never fully alongside car 41 so was not able to claim the right to the corner. “Through turn one, the driver of car 41 defended his position by releasing the brakes however [did] not force car 81 off the track, allowing racing room on the outside – which he is not required to do. “The stewards determined that the collision could have been avoided if the driver of car 81 had moved further to the left after turn one, even if this involved leaving the track prior to turn two.” Speaking before the stewards issued their decision Piastri said there was little he could have done to avoid the contact. “I obviously need to look back at it more,” he said, “but from in the car, I went to go up the inside of turn one Arvid moved very late and so I kind of ended up on the outside because I was avoiding him. And then from that point onwards, I tried to go around the outside. “He pushed me pretty wide and I was trying to back out and you where we made contact was well before the corner actually happened. So from my side of things I really didn’t have anywhere else to go.” Did the stewards issue the correct penalty? Cast your vote below and have your say in the comments. Piastri's penalty for colliding with Lindblad was: A RaceFans account is required in order to vote. If you do not have one, register an account here or read more about registering here . When this poll is closed the result will be displayed instead of the voting form. Having previously worked as a motoring journalist, Keith began running the site full-time in 2010, achieving a long-held ambition to dedicate his full attention to his passion for motor racing. View all posts by Keith Collantine Hilarious how this track with these cars is so awful for overtaking that Piastri could defend his position even with the damage he collected. He clearly had no pace, but still it was enough to defend his position. The same with Leclerc after the flat-spot. The idea of a multi-corner battle is dead with these racing regulations. All you have to do is dive super deep into the first in a series of corners and make the apex first, and suddenly, the bloke behind has no tools available to them. They either bail out, or in a vain attempt to hang around the outside, “cause” a collision when the defending car inevitably squeezes them off the road. That was the mistake Oscar made, instead of hanging around the outside and trying to overtake on track (god forbid!), he should’ve just skipped the corner like everyone else usually does and fired off down the road to try make up the five seconds! Never mind the ridiculous redesign of this track made before it returned to F1 a decade ago that made every corner into a tighter version of itself that reduces the number of viable lines and makes passing that much more difficult. So many outright anti-motor racing decisions being made in Formula 1 right now. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:23 @thexrod In fact, if you dive super deep into the first corner, and your opponent is outside of you, then your opponent is then blamed and penalised for anything that ensues. This appears to have happened at least twice this race, and it’s not the first times this year. (The Oscar Piastri case for me was more to do with Oscar attempting to make it “multi-corner” than anything else, which makes it especially germane to this point). Roger Ayles (@roger-ayles) 2nd November 2026, 2:32 The anti-racing overly bloated no room for common sense rulebook strikes again. Piastri may not have been ‘fully’ alongside at whatever point of the apex they look at but he was basically halfway alongside and therefore not only had a right to place his car there but also had a right to be given room and to continue the overtaking attempt into T2. The rules basically saying that because he wasn’t alongside the other cars mirror at the apex he no longer had a right to continue the overtaking attempt and even saying he should have left the track is yet more proof that these anti-racing regulations aren’t fit for purpose. The guidelines simply don’t suit situations like this. Sure if your not mostly alongside someone on the outside of say the Monaco hairpin then the overtaking attempt isn’t on. But if your even a bit alongside on the outside of a corner that leads into another where you’ll then be on the inside then the overtaking attempt is still very much on. I’m so sick of this nonsense now and going back and watching racing from not only other categories but also past decades of F1 just makes me even more sick of the joke guidelines F1 has now! Setting up an overtake by placing your car on the outside of the other car, thus compromising their line into the corner, then benefiting from it in the next corner, should be a legitimate maneuver in a race. The other car may or may not leave you enough space going into the corner – but you cannot predict that in advance. So, in the absence of mind-reading capabilities, your choice is either to expect being given room and continue with the maneuver; or expect to be squeezed out and automatically back out of the attempt. But if the latter is the required behaviour as per the rulebook (unless you are fully alongside), because it is you who’ll get penalized if the other driver ignores your physical presence on track , then the rulebook makes a legitimate motor racing maneuver practically impossible to carry out. Riker (@corsair) 2nd November 2026, 3:27 So…they expected.PIA to go off the track to avoid the collision when half good car was already off the track at the time? Really? No way is that a 10s penalty. Sigh. Riker (@corsair) 2nd November 2026, 3:28 Meant to say “half the car”. Silly auto correct. Leaving the track was literally the only way for him to avoid contact, while Lindblad could’ve avoided the contact by using more of the track width he had available. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:25 @corsair Yes. Apparently breaking the regulations is required to keep them. Juan Fanger (@juanfanger) 2nd November 2026, 5:30 David (@nvherman) 2nd November 2026, 7:16 Interesting to me that when Norris attempted to go around the outside of Leclerc at turn 5, no collision occurred. Yet again Piastri is involved in a collision because he doesn’t back out when the move isn’t on. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:28 @nvherman Interestingly, when Piastri did that to Leclerc at Spa earlier this year, no penalty was given to Piastri (and a few days later, the stewards claimed they should have penalised Leclerc. So the stewards’ stance in Spa likely led to Oscar thinking he was right to continue the fight in that moment in Mexico (if not afterwards). David (@nvherman) 2nd November 2026, 11:52 Interestingly, when Piastri did that to Leclerc at Spa earlier this year, no penalty was given to Piastri Thank you for reminding me of that incident. I’ve just rewatched it , and I believe that that was considered differently due to the contact happening in the braking zone (and Piastri was farther alongside in that incident, plus Leclerc was affected as regards to position or being able to continue). Linblad played stupid games and won a stupid prize. Ridiculous penalty, you can’t just kill racing through multiple corners like that I simply don’t comprehend the stewards’ argument, essentially claiming that Piastri should’ve left track limits to avoid contact, even though Lindblad could’ve equally avoided the contact by moving more to the right, which is what the stewards should point out rather than that Piastri could’ve moved more to the left, which itself is true, but would’ve required him to leave the track entirely, not to mention stewards typically want drivers to remain within track limits whenever possible & he could remain since he wasn’t forced off, so their argument is also contradictory. All in all, their verdicts & decisions on Leclerc, Russell, & Piastri were baffling. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:50 I feel like this whole situation could have been avoided, had the stewards not changed their verdict on the Piastri/Leclerc collision at Spa (presumably without evidence, as the change from “racing incident” to “Leclerc’s fault” was not accompanied by a penalty). That prevented Oscar from learning the right lessons from that crash and applying them here. How do I issue the FIA a 10-second penalty? Derek Warwick was one of this races Stewards…. says everything really. Rooie Piet (@axel3304) 2nd November 2026, 9:12 Racing incident at most. Ridiculous penalty which can only be defended by pointing to a set of guidelines which is time and time again proven to be woefully inadequate for judging incidents like this. They’re so hell-bent on concistency by applying black-and-white rules on grey areas that common sense is thrown out the window when judging an incident. Embarrassing. What are they supposed to do though? You complain that they shouldn’t apply black and white rules to a grey area, but then complain about bias or unequal treatment if they don’t then apply those same rules to every driver in a consistent way. Are they supposed to apply the rules equally to all, or are they meant to ignore the rules if it’s a more popular driver who ends up on the receiving end of that penalty? Is it really about “common sense”, or a sense of outrage that they dared to penalise Piastri when he’s more popular than Lindblad? Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:51 Unfortunately this approach means they also get accused of bias and inconsistency, since the stewards have demonstrably not been consistent between Piastri/Lindblad in Mexico and Piastri/Leclerc in Spa. Piastri’s penalty for colliding with Lindblad was…. …Given too late. Somehow F1 refereeing seems like a comitee having endless meetings about something that can be just straightforward. They should stop listening to the teams and drivers. And only judge the actions as they are. And if they cannot do that in reasonable time, they should spend some of those billions to make sure they can. Unless they can invent a time machine, that would be physically impossible regardless of how much was spent. If you can’t perform a task in a timely manner, you could: Improve the way of working Use better tools Hire more colleagues The FOM has their new operating centre for about a week. I’ll be curious to see if this will show in faster decision making. In Mexico there were still plenty too much after the race finished. https://www.racefans.net/2026/10/21/fias-new-formula-1-race-operations-centre-opens-at-foms-biggin-hil

items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri is set to start the Mexico City Grand Prix from P13 after poor Qualifying. His pace looked promising though, he finished Q1 fourth, but after aborting his final Q2 effort he wasn’t quick enough to make it in Q3.
